title: Guide: Three Simple, Robust Methods for Establishing Value in the First Weeks of School eks-of-school/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This guide addresses the Value belief — a student's sense that the work matters — which Stuart ranks as the second most powerful of the five key beliefs after Credibility. Stuart frames Value as a 'rainbow' belief because students arrive at it through many routes: utility, intrinsic interest, identity, challenge, fun, and meaning. He cautions against mono-chromatic approaches that rely on a single angle (such as cultural relevance), arguing that diverse classrooms require diverse pathways to value. The three recommended strategies are: exposing students to compelling examples of disciplinary work, using Chris Hulleman's Build Connections intervention, and connecting learning to students' identities and long-term goals. The article positions Value as a prerequisite for Belonging, Effort, and Efficacy — if a student sees no worth in the content, those other motivational levers have nothing to act on.
points: Value is a 'rainbow' belief — students arrive at it through utility, interest, identity, meaning, challenge, and fun — so teachers should play to multiple pathways simultaneously
Credibility is prerequisite to Value: students are more open to finding meaning in work when they already believe the teacher is competent and caring
Mono-chromatic approaches to relevance (e.g., always tying content to pop culture) are insufficient for diverse classrooms; multiple value angles must be pursued
Chris Hulleman's Build Connections intervention asks students to link course content to their own lives and goals, producing measurable motivation gains
Without the Value belief, the other four beliefs have no foundation: a student who sees no worth in the subject has no reason to care about belonging or succeeding in it
